Hello homebrewers! I'm an aspiring home brewer (I was recently hired by a beer company, so I figure its my duty to do this as a hobby now) and I'm looking to get started with extract to get familiar with the process before moving on to BIAB or All-Grain brews.

I've got my eyes on a "starter kit," that is fairly comprehensive, and then adding some basics that I think are helpful.

I chose the Brewers Best Deluxe Starter Kit: http://www.amazon.com/Brewers-Best-DELUXE-Brewing-Equipment/dp/B00AC55H24 because for the purchase price it has a lot of useful things. Compared to their basic kit, it has a lot of convenience items like the auto siphon and the price at my home brew store is not that bad.

In addition to this starter kit, I planned on getting a 20 quart pot as well as a floating thermometer, beer thief, carboy carrier, and of course the ingredient kit.

I think this is a good starting point, because its easy to use the fermenting equipment for BIAB brewing later, simply by upgrading the stock pot and getting a larger burner.

What would you suggest as your absolutely must have items for a beginner?

As much as I would love to have one of the brew pots with a false bottom and spigot and a cooler mashtun, I think that's out of my depth for right now :) I don't even need a wort chiller, do I?
Just getting started, have I forgotten anything?

• Are your going to be bringing it to a boil and then adding hops? If so you will need a method of rapidly cooling it to pitching temp. Some people get by without a wort chiller (ice bath etc), but for convenience and best results a wort chiller is the way to go. You can build your won easily enough

  • You will also need bottles and caps, but they are easy enough to get hold of

There are a LOT of opinions on how to brew, this is just what I've worked out for my own extract brews after ~15 years (yes, I extract brew most of my beer as AG just doesn't provide enough return on the time invested):

Boil pot, make sure it's stainless and NOT aluminum. I'm currently using a Keggle but started with boiling half-batches in a ~16quart stockpot.

I boil outside on propane now (faster, easier cleanup if I make a mess), but the kitchen range was where I started.

I use a counter-flow chiller to cool the wort after boiling now, but in the beginning I used the sink half-full of salted ice water and the remaining half of my water (because I only boiled 2.5 gallons) was just above freezing. I no longer use a thermometer at all, I'm either heating/boiling or chilling... but in the beginning I used a normal kitchen thermometer to see the wort temp while cooling (aiming for ~110F so when combined with 40F water it'd be about pitching temp once combined).

Today I have an oxygen stone to oxygenate the wort (made an Amazing difference), though I used to just shake the crap out of the carboy and splash the wort as much as possible while adding it to the carboy.

Today I have a wort cooler (freezer with temp controller) that I just put my 6.5gal carboy into and wait for temps to stabilize before pitching yeast ~ I've left it for more than a day when I simply ran out of time. In the beginning I'd just wait a few minutes for the stick-on carboy thermometer to stabilize and then pitch the yeast. I've pretty much always used liquid yeast (only the very first time did I use dry), and prefer the Wyeast "smack packs" since they are basically their own starter and you KNOW it's viable before pitching. I have made starters, and they made a difference, but fall into the same category as AG, not enough return on the time invested.

I have 3 5-gallon carboys that haven't been used in years. I simply do not rack to secondary anymore after reading up on the topic. It's a non-issue for 5-gallon sizes in carboys and buckets ~ waste of money to buy one unless you're going to try and use it for smaller batches ~ at least IMHO.

I do use a beer/wine thief for taking samples to do my gravity tests with Hydrometer and test vessel (usually only 2, the OG and then 7~10 days later the FG).

I do love my auto-siphon, though the plastic racking cane always breaks so I simply replace it with a SS racking cane (meaning it's still an auto-siphon, I simply swap out the plastic piece for SS when it breaks). And I finally, I haven't bottled since my very first batch, it was such a nightmare that I immediately moved into kegging.

So, to me it looks like you'd be buying stuff you won't use/don't need (both in the kit and out of it). But you do have all the basics covered for equipment. What I've got to wonder though, is if you're working for a brewery there HAS to be someone else who homebrews there. Someone who will loan you all of their equipment and mentor you on your first brew... maybe even gift (or sell) you the stuff you need if you want to own everything straight away. I know I'm more than willing to let someone use my setup to brew, free the first time then consumable costs (propane and electrical, about $10) after that. It's certainly more fun to brew with someone else, and the enthusiasm and excitement of someone new can be infectious for those of us who have been doing it awhile. Otherwise there are always people selling these same starter kits on craigslist, I've seen some for $20. Means more money for kits if you don't have to buy everything new... :)

What is the disadvantage of an aluminum brewpot?

The biggest is that it gives the beer a metallic "off" flavor, but there's some debate over it contributing to alzheimers too. Both can supposedly be mitigated by building up an oxidization layer, but that layer is easily scratched while stirring or removed from cleaning.

It's just one of those things that has unwanted (and unknown) variables that You can eliminate. I see it as wearing a seatbelt while in a car ~ probably not going to have any issues, but why take the risk?

Opinions are going to very widely on this because everyone's brewing method is a little different. As far as bang for your buck, the two most important things you can buy that you don't have already are an in-line carbon filter (if there is chlorine in your tap water) and an immersion chiller. The carbon filter is like $10 and will help you get rid of an off flavor (chlorophenols) that some 90% of homebrews I try seem to have. In fact, I thought of the off flavor as "that homebrew taste" for a while until I learned what it was. An immersion chiller will dramatically increase the quality of your beer, as well as helping to prevent infected batches (less time exposing your post-boil wort to the microbe-filled air). I don't even brew in the summer, because (among other reasons) my groundwater is too hot to quickly cool a batch. An immersion chiller is going to be $50 - $100, so maybe not as important right away as a carbon filter. Hope this helps...
